title: How Do We Know It Worked?

scenes.tts: The first film built a blue plasmid carrying a green insulin gene. Now how do we know that change worked? A surviving bacterial colony is evidence, but evidence for which claim? Follow the same plasmid onto a testing bench.
scenes.caption: The first film built a blue plasmid carrying a green insulin gene. Now how do we know that change worked? A surviving bacterial colony is evidence, but evidence for which claim? Follow the same plasmid onto a testing bench.
scenes.visual: Hook first. Rebuild the first film's large blue plasmid with green gene, then slide it onto a wide teal testing bench. A gray colony grows beside three empty claim frames. Reuse exactly: blue plasmid, green intended gene or edit, yellow tools, red selection or risk, teal evidence, purple values. Label noncomputed imagery 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The first film built a blue plasmid carrying a green insulin gene. Now how do we know that change worked? A surviving bacterial colony is evidence, but evidence for which claim? Follow the same plasmid onto a testing bench.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: How Do We Know It Worked? The blue-green plasmid continues turning slowly behind the title.

scenes.tts: One engineered bacterium can support several different claims. It may have taken up a plasmid. That plasmid may contain the intended insulin D N A. The cell may also read the gene and make insulin protein. Each claim needs its own test. A check mark belongs to a claim, not to the whole organism.
scenes.caption: One engineered bacterium can support several different claims. It may have taken up a plasmid. That plasmid may contain the intended insulin DNA. The cell may also read the gene and make insulin protein. Each claim needs its own test. A check mark belongs to a claim, not to the whole organism.
scenes.visual: The one colony expands to fill the left half. Three large claim frames stack on the right: plasmid taken up, insulin DNA present, insulin protein made. Teal question marks orbit inside the frames while the colony gently grows.
scenes.narration: One engineered bacterium can support several different claims. It may have taken up a plasmid. That plasmid may contain the intended insulin DNA. The cell may also read the gene and make insulin protein. Each claim needs its own test. A check mark belongs to a claim, not to the whole organism.

scenes.tts: Keep the blue plasmid and green product separate in your answer. Predict before opening the first frame. A colony grows on antibiotic because the plasmid carries resistance. Does that growth alone prove the bacterium is making insulin?
scenes.caption: Keep the blue plasmid and green product separate in your answer. Predict before opening the first frame. A colony grows on antibiotic because the plasmid carries resistance. Does that growth alone prove the bacterium is making insulin?
scenes.visual: Move the colony onto a large red antibiotic plate. The blue plasmid remains visible inside the cell; a separate dashed green product outline stays outside. Put the question overhead without revealing any check mark.
scenes.narration: Keep the blue plasmid and green product separate in your answer. Predict before opening the first frame. A colony grows on antibiotic because the plasmid carries resistance. Does that growth alone prove the bacterium is making insulin?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question. The red plate shimmers, the colony grows slightly, and the dashed green product outline remains unresolved.

scenes.tts: No. Antibiotic growth supports plasmid uptake because resistance travels on that plasmid. The insulin insert might still be missing, reversed, or unread. Selection narrows the cells worth testing. It does not replace the tests.
scenes.caption: No. Antibiotic growth supports plasmid uptake because resistance travels on that plasmid. The insulin insert might still be missing, reversed, or unread. Selection narrows the cells worth testing. It does not replace the tests.
scenes.visual: A teal check enters only the first claim frame, plasmid taken up. The second and third frames keep question marks. The colony and plate shrink to the bench's left end while a yellow test tool rolls in from the right.
scenes.narration: No. Antibiotic growth supports plasmid uptake because resistance travels on that plasmid. The insulin insert might still be missing, reversed, or unread. Selection narrows the cells worth testing. It does not replace the tests.

scenes.tts: Next test the D N A. The polymerase chain reaction copies one chosen stretch. A gel sorts D N A pieces by size, with shorter pieces traveling farther. An expected band supports the insert's presence and size. Sequencing can confirm its identity.
scenes.caption: Next test the DNA. The polymerase chain reaction copies one chosen stretch. A gel sorts DNA pieces by size, with shorter pieces traveling farther. An expected band supports the insert's presence and size. Sequencing can confirm its identity.
scenes.visual: Transform the yellow tool into a schematic copying gate labeled 'ideal PCR model' that doubles green DNA blocks; a small on-screen note says real copying is less than perfect. Blocks flow into a large gel. Compute only their screen positions from assigned sizes; short blocks travel farther. Label the gel 'schematic sizes' and add a teal check to the DNA claim.
scenes.narration: Next test the DNA. The polymerase chain reaction copies one chosen stretch. A gel sorts DNA pieces by size, with shorter pieces traveling farther. An expected band supports the insert's presence and size. Sequencing can confirm its identity.

scenes.tts: A D N A band still does not show insulin protein. Use a protein test, including an empty-plasmid control and a known insulin sample. A signal in the engineered group, with controls behaving correctly, supports production. Purity and function need further tests.
scenes.caption: A DNA band still does not show insulin protein. Use a protein test, including an empty-plasmid control and a known insulin sample. A signal in the engineered group, with controls behaving correctly, supports production. Purity and function need further tests.
scenes.visual: The gel slides left. Three large wells appear: engineered cells, empty plasmid, known insulin. Teal signals rise only in the engineered and known-sample wells. The third claim frame receives a teal check; smaller question marks move onward to purity and function.
scenes.narration: A DNA band still does not show insulin protein. Use a protein test, including an empty-plasmid control and a known insulin sample. A signal in the engineered group, with controls behaving correctly, supports production. Purity and function need further tests.

scenes.tts: The same logic follows other uses. A crop, an edited blood stem cell, and a research cell each begin with a specific change. Measure the intended effect, possible unintended effects, and limits. Do not transfer one result to every use.
scenes.caption: The same logic follows other uses. A crop, an edited blood stem cell, and a research cell each begin with a specific change. Measure the intended effect, possible unintended effects, and limits. Do not transfer one result to every use.
scenes.visual: The evidence bench widens without cutting away. The blue-green test object transforms into three large schematic cards: crop, blood stem cell, research cell. Teal measuring brackets inspect effects while red question marks remain beside possible unintended effects and limits.
scenes.narration: The same logic follows other uses. A crop, an edited blood stem cell, and a research cell each begin with a specific change. Measure the intended effect, possible unintended effects, and limits. Do not transfer one result to every use.

scenes.tts: Consider the lesson's crop survey. Its lines rise as the share of corn and soybean acres planted with engineered varieties grows. Those data show adoption. They do not show safety, environmental effect, farmer benefit, or fairness. Those claims require other evidence.
scenes.caption: Consider the lesson's crop survey. Its lines rise as the share of corn and soybean acres planted with engineered varieties grows. Those data show adoption. They do not show safety, environmental effect, farmer benefit, or fairness. Those claims require other evidence.
scenes.visual: Transform the crop card into a large two-line chart computed from these lesson data. Years: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2010, 2016, 2020, 2024, 2025. Corn percentages: 25, 47, 80, 86, 92, 92, 94, 94. Soybean percentages: 54, 85, 92, 93, 94, 94, 96, 96. Put only endpoint values and years on screen. Title the chart 'adoption'. Separate red question frames for safety, environment, benefit, and fairness stay outside the plot.
scenes.narration: Consider the lesson's crop survey. Its lines rise as the share of corn and soybean acres planted with engineered varieties grows. Those data show adoption. They do not show safety, environmental effect, farmer benefit, or fairness. Those claims require other evidence.

scenes.tts: Evidence can estimate benefits and risks, but it cannot choose every value. Ask who wrote the claim, what evidence supports it, and whether other scientists checked it. Then discuss access, safety, and limits for that particular use. Reasonable people may weigh the same evidence differently.
scenes.caption: Evidence can estimate benefits and risks, but it cannot choose every value. Ask who wrote the claim, what evidence supports it, and whether other scientists checked it. Then discuss access, safety, and limits for that particular use. Reasonable people may weigh the same evidence differently.
scenes.visual: The plot and three use cards settle beneath two large lenses. A teal evidence lens checks source, support, and review. A purple values lens brings forward access, safety, and limits. Both lenses focus on one use card at a time.
scenes.narration: Evidence can estimate benefits and risks, but it cannot choose every value. Ask who wrote the claim, what evidence supports it, and whether other scientists checked it. Then discuss access, safety, and limits for that particular use. Reasonable people may weigh the same evidence differently.

scenes.tts: A changed D N A sequence is the start of an explanation, not the end. Match each claim to a test, keep uncertainty visible, and judge cases one by one. Engineering changes a cell's D N A; test the effects, judge each use separately.
scenes.caption: A changed DNA sequence is the start of an explanation, not the end. Match each claim to a test, keep uncertainty visible, and judge cases one by one. Engineering changes a cell's DNA; test the effects, judge each use separately.
scenes.visual: Compress the entire bench into a moving chain: blue-green change, teal tests, checked effect, then evidence and values lenses around one use. Leave red uncertainty marks where questions remain. The chain fills most of the frame.
scenes.narration: A changed DNA sequence is the start of an explanation, not the end. Match each claim to a test, keep uncertainty visible, and judge cases one by one. Engineering changes a cell's DNA; test the effects, judge each use separately.

scenes.visual: End card with one line only, centered and large: 'Engineering changes a cell's DNA; test the effects, judge each use separately.' No subtitle, title, logo line, or smaller text.
